items.name: Readability
items.evidence: No saved script. All logic ran as inline `python3 -c` one-liners with terse names (`dec`, `f`, `s1`, `v1`, `h_c1`). They are readable enough but not documented or reusable. The diff only contains the binary WAL and recovered.json.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: The project asks for a short, re-runnable decrypt script plus an extraction step. The agent left neither, only ad-hoc inline commands (step 38 decrypts, writes the WAL and dumps JSON in one go). The XOR loop was copy-pasted across steps 10–38. No scratch-file mess, though.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The final step hardcodes `b ^ 0x42` with no in-script check of the magic bytes after decryption and no error handling. Mitigations: it validated checksums beforehand, opened the db read-only, and asserted the JSON output afterwards (step 49).

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The decrypted header matched magic 0x377f0682 (0x75^0x37=0x42). It verified the header and all 4 frame checksums (step 13, match=True), let SQLite replay the WAL on a test copy, then checked the count was 11 and asserted the JSON.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: Step 1 backed up main.db.bak and main.db-wal.bak before anything else. That mattered: the read-write `sqlite3 .tables` in step 4 deleted the encrypted WAL, and the fix was rebuilt from the .bak. Note: the backups were removed at the end.
